claims.text: Directional solidification of a W–Cu composite can produce aligned, continuous copper pathways.
Aligned, continuous copper pathways will increase thermal conductivity relative to a conventionally processed W–Cu composite with randomly dispersed copper.
The directionally solidified composite will retain mechanical durability relative to the conventional W–Cu composite.
The directionally solidified composite will retain irradiation resistance relative to the conventional W–Cu composite.
Typical W–Cu composites have a randomly distributed copper phase within a tungsten matrix.
A randomly distributed W–Cu composite offers moderate thermal conductivity.
A randomly distributed W–Cu composite offers acceptable mechanical durability and irradiation resistance.
Fusion-reactor materials must operate under high temperature, high heat flux, and intense high-energy neutron flux.
The proposed effect will hold under cyclic high-temperature loading.
Continuous, aligned copper pathways will facilitate electron transport by reducing interface scattering.
Reduced electron scattering in the aligned copper pathways will increase effective thermal conductivity.
The tungsten matrix will continue to provide mechanical stability after directional solidification.
The tungsten matrix will continue to provide irradiation resistance after directional solidification.
Directional solidification will improve thermal conductivity by roughly 20% or more relative to an isotropic W–Cu composite.
The thermal-conductivity improvement will occur without a significant loss of mechanical strength.
The thermal-conductivity improvement will occur without a significant loss of irradiation resilience.
Poor interfacial bonding or deleterious microstructural features could prevent the proposed benefit.
Failure to achieve an approximately 20% or greater statistically significant thermal-conductivity increase would falsify the hypothesis.
Notable deterioration in mechanical durability or irradiation resistance would falsify the hypothesis.
